_note: Source for tools/generate-csmath-kits.mjs (briefs + rubrics) and tools/make-workbooks.py (practice + exemplar workbooks). One kit per cornerstone: concept decks, a practice workbook, an interactive tool, the build brief, and a four-level exemplar set. `rubricSpine` is the shared default rubric; a kit may override it with its own `rubrics` array (Cornerstone I carries two — one for the final spreadsheet, one for the final presentation).

levels.name: Advanced
levels.gloss: Publishable. Someone else could pick this up and use it.

levels.name: Proficient
levels.gloss: Works and is honest. The expected standard.

levels.name: Developing
levels.gloss: Partly works, or works for the wrong reasons.

levels.name: Beginning
levels.gloss: Incomplete, or the numbers cannot be trusted.

criteria.name: Model Correctness
criteria.question: Does it compute the right answer, for the right reason?

d.1: Outputs are wrong, missing, or cannot be recomputed from the inputs shown.
d.2: Outputs are correct for the one case that was tested. Changing an input breaks something or produces a silently wrong number.
d.3: Outputs are correct for reasonable inputs. The model holds together when assumptions are changed.
d.4: Every output is correct and stays correct when inputs change. Edge cases (zero, negative, extreme values) behave sensibly or are explicitly blocked.

criteria.name: Formula Honesty
criteria.question: Is the arithmetic real, or is it typed in?

d.1: Key results are typed in. Changing an input does not change the answer — the model is a picture of a model.
d.2: Some results are typed in rather than computed, or magic numbers are buried inside formulas. Rounding is applied inconsistently.
d.3: Formulas do the work; inputs live in their own cells. Any constant is a genuine constant and is labelled.
d.4: Nothing is hard-coded that should be computed. Every assumption is a labelled input cell that the formulas reference. Precision claimed matches precision earned.

criteria.name: Data Structure
criteria.question: Could a stranger navigate this file?

d.1: No discernible structure. The reader cannot tell what is an input, what is a result, or what is scratch.
d.2: Organisation is inconsistent — inputs mixed with results, unlabelled columns, stray working cells left in place.
d.3: Logical tab and column organisation with clear headers. A reader can find the inputs and follow the calculation.
d.4: Inputs, calculations, and outputs are cleanly separated. Tabs, headers, and named ranges make intent obvious without explanation. Consistent formatting throughout.

criteria.name: Communication
criteria.question: Does the chart and the write-up tell the truth clearly?

d.1: No chart, or a chart that cannot be read. No stated conclusion.
d.2: Charts exist but mislead or decorate — truncated axes, wrong chart type, missing labels. The write-up describes what was built rather than what it means.
d.3: Charts are appropriate and labelled. The write-up states the conclusion and the main assumptions.
d.4: Charts are chosen for the question being answered, axes are labelled and honest, and the write-up states the conclusion, the assumptions behind it, and what would change it.

criteria.name: Stretch
criteria.question: Optional — did you push past the floor?

d.1: Not attempted (no penalty — this criterion is optional).
d.2: Stretch attempted but incomplete or not integrated with the main model.
d.4: Extends the model in a way that answers a new question, and explains why the extension was worth building.

kits.title: The Toolbox
kits.premise: Before we model anything, we agree on the language: notation, estimation, and the parts of a spreadsheet.
kits.evidence: A short skills check rather than a model: notation read correctly, an estimate justified, and a lookup that returns the right value.

kits.title: Food & Macro Tracker
kits.premise: Track what you actually eat for two weeks, source where every macro number comes from, then build the model that turns that log into an answer about yourself.

decks.title: The Data You Generate
decks.concept: Every model starts as a table someone had to design — and every macro you log was looked up somewhere. Rows are observations, columns are variables, and a number without a source is a rumor. This deck also runs the preview activity and the dataset-download walkthrough.

decks.title: Lookup & Aggregate
decks.concept: Two moves do most of the work in every model this year: fetch a fact from a reference table (VLOOKUP — including a second lookup that returns each food's source), and summarise many rows into one number (SUMIF/AVERAGEIF). Then turn the aggregate into one honest chart that states a finding.

practicum.title: Lookup & Aggregate Practice
drills: Given a 15-food reference table, return the calories for a named food — then break it on purpose by misspelling the name, and fix it with IFERROR.
Total calories for a single day using SUMIF; then average across days with AVERAGEIF.
Add a food to the reference table and confirm every downstream number updates without editing a formula.
Find the deliberately planted hard-coded cell and replace it with a formula.

tool.title: Macro Explorer
tool.job: Log foods and watch macros recompute live; drag a portion slider to see how one change ripples through daily totals, and watch the source-mix bar show how much of today's calories came from your least reliable sources. Students meet the behaviour before they build the mechanism.

kits.evidence: Two deliverables. (1) A working spreadsheet over ≥14 days of your own logged data: a reference table with a Source for every food, a daily log where VLOOKUP fills the macros and the source, SUMIF/AVERAGEIF aggregation into a dashboard, and one honest chart. (2) A short presentation of one insight about your own eating — a specific claim your data supports, the evidence behind it, and the caveat that would change it.
kits.stretch: Add a second reference table (cost per serving) and answer a second question: what does a day of your eating cost — and is the cheapest day also the most trustworthy data?

exemplarPresentation.title: 14 Days, One Question — exemplar presentation
exemplarPresentation.job: A full student presentation that earns a 4.0 on the presentation rubric: the insight is stated up front, every claim is traceable to the model, the chart is honest, and the caveat is named. Read it before you build your own.

handouts.label: Mini-brief & preview activity
handouts.note: the one-page project brief, the *Source Three Foods* preview activity, the dataset-download steps, and the source color key

rubrics.title: Final Spreadsheet
rubrics.note: The tracker itself, scored out of 4.0. A 4.0 is a spreadsheet someone else could open, trust, and reuse — not one that happens to print the right number today.

levels.name: Advanced
levels.gloss: Publishable. Someone else could pick this up and use it.

levels.name: Proficient
levels.gloss: Works and is honest. The expected standard.

levels.name: Developing
levels.gloss: Partly works, or works for the wrong reasons.

levels.name: Beginning
levels.gloss: Incomplete, or the numbers cannot be trusted.

criteria.name: Data Design
criteria.question: Are the rows, columns, and reference table designed so the model can answer a question?

d.1: No coherent table — foods, servings, and macros are typed wherever they fit. Nothing can be recomputed.
d.2: Foods, servings, and macros are mixed together, or the table cannot grow without rework. Some headers have no units.
d.3: A workable reference table and log with clear, unit-labelled headers; minor inconsistencies but the structure holds.
d.4: Every food is one row; the reference table holds one serving's macros and a source for each food; every column is labelled with its unit; the design scales as the log grows.

criteria.name: Sourcing & Trust
criteria.question: Does every macro's origin travel with the number?

d.1: No source recorded anywhere — the numbers are unattributed and uncheckable.
d.2: Sources recorded for some foods, or recorded but never color-coded; no sense that sources differ in trustworthiness.
d.3: Sources are recorded and color-coded for most foods, and the write-up acknowledges that estimates are weaker than labels.
d.4: Every food's Source is recorded and color-coded with the key, and the write-up names which sources are weakest and why that matters to the conclusion.

criteria.name: Lookup & Aggregate Correctness
criteria.question: Do VLOOKUP, SUMIF, and AVERAGEIF compute the right answer, for the right reason?

d.1: Numbers are typed in; no working lookup or aggregation.
d.2: Some formulas work for the one row that was tested; a renamed food or a new log row breaks the sheet silently.
d.3: Lookups return the right macro and source for the log as built; SUMIF/AVERAGEIF are correct and adding a row works.
d.4: Every lookup returns the right macro and source; SUMIF per day and AVERAGEIF across days stay correct when a food is renamed, a source changes, or rows are added.

criteria.name: Formula Honesty
criteria.question: Is the arithmetic real, or is it typed in?

d.1: Key results are typed in. Changing an input changes nothing — the sheet is a picture of a model.
d.2: Some results are typed in rather than computed, or magic numbers are buried inside formulas.
d.3: Formulas do the work; inputs (servings, targets) live in their own labelled cells. Any constant is a genuine, labelled constant.
d.4: Nothing is hard-coded that should be computed; servings and targets are labelled inputs the formulas reference; the whole model recalculates cleanly from the source table.

criteria.name: Chart & Insight
criteria.question: Does the chart answer your question, and does the write-up say what it means?

d.1: No chart, or an unreadable one; no stated insight.
d.2: A chart exists but misleads or decorates — truncated axis, wrong chart type, missing labels. The write-up describes what was built rather than what it means.
d.3: The chart is appropriate and labelled with units; the insight is stated, if not quantified.
d.4: The chart is chosen for the question, axes labelled with units and honest, and the write-up states a specific insight the data supports plus the caveat that would change it.

criteria.name: Stretch
criteria.question: Optional — did you push past the floor?

d.1: Not attempted (no penalty — this criterion is optional).
d.2: The cost table is attempted but not integrated, or the second question is answered with a typed number.
d.3: The second reference table is built correctly and its question is answered with a computed figure.
d.4: The cost extension answers a genuinely new question and explains why it was worth building — including whether the cheapest day was also the best-sourced.

rubrics.title: Final Presentation
rubrics.note: The presentation of your findings, scored out of 4.0. The model is only half the deliverable — the other half is whether you can tell someone what it means.

levels.name: Advanced
levels.gloss: The audience leaves knowing something about you they did not know before.

levels.name: Proficient
levels.gloss: Clear, supported, and honest. The expected standard.

levels.name: Developing
levels.gloss: A tour of the spreadsheet with a finding attached.

criteria.name: The Insight
criteria.question: Is there a real, specific claim about your own eating — or just a walkthrough?

d.1: No finding stated; the presentation describes the file.
d.2: A claim is made but the data does not support it, or it is so broad it cannot be wrong.
d.3: A clear claim is stated and supported by the model, if broad.
d.4: Opens with a specific, non-obvious claim the data supports (e.g. restaurant days are 78% of my over-target days, and they are also my least reliable rows) — a claim that could have been wrong.

criteria.name: Evidence & Honesty
criteria.question: Can the audience trace the claim to the numbers, and do you name the uncertainty?

d.1: No evidence; claims are unconnected to the data.
d.2: The claim is asserted without the number, or the number cannot be found in the model.
d.3: The evidence is shown and traceable to the model; the main assumption is stated.
d.4: The number behind the claim is shown and traceable; the weakest sources are named; what would change the conclusion is stated explicitly.

criteria.name: Visuals
criteria.question: Do the charts earn their place and tell the truth?

d.1: No chart, or one that cannot be read.
d.2: Charts are crowded, mislabelled, or decorative.
d.3: Charts are appropriate and labelled with units.
d.4: One or two charts, chosen for the question, labelled with units, honest axes, and readable from the back of the room.

criteria.name: Delivery
criteria.question: Could a listener follow it without seeing the file?

d.2: Reads the slides, runs long or short, or jumps around.
d.3: Organized and on time; mostly spoken rather than read.
d.4: A clear arc (question → method → finding → caveat), within time, spoken not read, with any key term defined the moment it is used.

criteria.name: Response to Questions
criteria.question: Can you defend the model and its assumptions?

d.2: Cannot locate a number in the model or defend an assumption.
d.3: Answers reasonably and can point to where a number comes from.
d.4: Answers with reference to the model; distinguishes what is known from what is assumed; names a limit or a next step.

criteria.name: Stretch
criteria.question: Optional — did you push past the floor?

d.1: Not attempted (no penalty — this criterion is optional).
d.2: A second question is mentioned but not shown.
d.3: A second question is answered with its own evidence.
d.4: A second question is answered and connected back to the first — showing how the two findings explain each other.

kits.title: Financing a Car
kits.premise: Interest is the same machine whether it is paying you or charging you. Meet it as a friend first, then as a creditor.

decks.title: Interest Works For You First
decks.concept: Before borrowing, save. A high-yield savings account is compound interest pointed at you: the same formula, the same curve, the opposite sign. Understanding growth from the friendly side makes the amortisation table obvious instead of frightening.

decks.title: The Amortisation Machine
decks.concept: A loan payment is one number that hides two: interest owed on the remaining balance, and principal that actually reduces it. Watching the split shift month by month is the whole lesson.

practicum.title: HYSA → Loan Practice
drills: HYSA: $500 at 4.5% APY, compounded monthly. Build the growth table for 5 years and chart it.
Change compounding from monthly to daily. Explain in one sentence why the difference is small.
Now flip the sign: the same machine as a $12,000 loan at 7% for 60 months. Build the payment formula.
Split one payment into interest and principal. Copy down 60 rows and chart the crossover.
Compare a 60-month and a 72-month loan on total interest paid. Which is the bigger number, and why is the smaller monthly payment the more expensive choice?

tool.title: Car Loan Amortisation Calculator
tool.job: Slide MSRP, down payment, rate, and term; watch monthly payment, total interest, and the down-payment comparison update. The amortisation table is the answer key students rebuild in Excel.

kits.evidence: A model that takes MSRP, down payment, rate, and term as inputs and produces the monthly payment, a full amortisation schedule, and a defended recommendation of which financing option you would actually take.
kits.stretch: Port the amortisation schedule to Python (a starting script ships with the kit) and confirm both produce the same payment to the cent.

kits.title: Personal Budget
kits.premise: You graduate, you get a job in Miami, and you pick a neighborhood. The rent is real, the salary is real, and the month does not care about your plan. Build the budget that survives it.

decks.title: The Hand You're Dealt
decks.concept: Fixed versus variable cost is the distinction the whole model turns on. Your randomly assigned role and neighborhood set the income and the rent — what you can change and what you cannot sets the strategy.

decks.title: Scenarios & the Savings Rate
decks.concept: A budget that only works in the expected month is not a budget. Scenario columns turn one plan into a stress test, and the savings rate is the single number that says whether you are actually getting ahead.

practicum.title: Miami Young-Professional Budget Practice
drills: Roll your life: the randomiser assigns a job title, a starting salary, a Miami neighborhood, and a student-loan balance. Everyone gets a different hand, so nobody can copy.
Look up your neighborhood's real median rent from the reference table and pull it in with a lookup — do not type it.
Convert gross salary to take-home: federal tax, FICA, and the fact that Florida has no state income tax. Explain what that last one is worth to you in dollars per month.
Classify twelve expenses as fixed or variable — then defend two you found genuinely ambiguous.
Build the savings rate as a formula, not a typed number.

Draw a scenario: the randomiser fires a Miami curveball (hurricane deductible, car repair on the 826, rent hike at renewal, hours cut, a bonus). Show the month under baseline and under the curveball, side by side.
Find the break point — how many months of the bad scenario before savings hit zero?

tool.title: Budget Scenario Lab
tool.job: Rolls a young-professional life in Miami — job title, salary, neighborhood, student debt — then fires random local curveballs and shows the month under each scenario with a live savings-rate meter and a months-to-zero readout. Generates each student's unique starting hand.

kits.evidence: A budget model built on your assigned Miami hand: take-home pay derived from gross, neighborhood rent pulled by lookup, categorised spending, a computed savings rate, at least three scenarios including one that breaks the budget, and a stated plan for the break.
kits.stretch: Compare two neighborhoods on the same salary. Does the cheaper rent actually win once commute cost and time are priced in?

kits.title: The Casino Lab
kits.premise: Randomness is not chaos. Run it enough times and it becomes the most predictable thing in the room.

decks.title: Expected Value & the House Edge
decks.concept: Expected value is what one play is worth on average — and the house edge is why 'on average' beats 'lucky' over a long enough night. This is the bridge to every simulation that follows.

practicum.title: Simulation Practice
drills: RAND and RANDBETWEEN: simulate one coin flip, then 10, then 1,000.
Compute expected value for a simple bet by hand, then simulate it and compare.
Chart the running average across 1,000 trials and watch it settle — the law of large numbers, seen.
Model a real casino game's house edge and compute expected loss per hour of play.

tool.title: Law of Large Numbers Simulator
tool.job: Run 10, 100, 1,000, or 100,000 trials of a chosen bet and watch the running average converge on expected value in real time. The point students cannot get from a static deck: small samples lie, large ones do not.
tool.priority: Build before Cornerstone IV — the Monte Carlo work in Stocks assumes this intuition is already in place.

kits.evidence: A simulation of a chosen game with computed expected value, a convergence chart, and a one-paragraph explanation of why the house always wins in the long run.
kits.stretch: Simulate a betting strategy (martingale, flat betting) and show whether it changes expected value. It does not — prove it.

kits.title: Stocks: Forecasting & Management
kits.premise: You are handed $100,000 of simulated capital on Investopedia and a market that does not care what you think. Research across verticals, take real positions, and defend them with a model.

decks.title: Returns & Volatility
decks.concept: A return is percent change; volatility is how much those changes scatter. Together they are the two numbers that describe any asset — and the inputs to every forecast you will build.

decks.title: Monte Carlo Forecasting
decks.concept: You cannot predict one future, so simulate a thousand. The casino's tools aimed at your own portfolio: a distribution of outcomes instead of a single misleading number — and a way to judge your Investopedia trades that is not just "did it go up".

practicum.title: Research, Returns & Simulation Practice
drills: Open the Investopedia simulator and take one position. Record why you bought it BEFORE you know what happens.
Pull a price history and compute daily returns as percent change.
Build a moving average and explain what it hides as well as what it shows.
Compute volatility as the standard deviation of returns — then compare a utility stock against a growth stock and describe the difference in one sentence.
Run a one-year Monte Carlo forecast from those two numbers and chart the spread of outcomes.
Report the 10th, 50th, and 90th percentile outcome — and explain why quoting only the median is dishonest.

tool.title: Portfolio Monte Carlo
tool.job: Set starting capital at $100,000, choose an allocation across verticals, and run thousands of paths to see the distribution of outcomes rather than a single line. Makes the fan chart intuitive before Excel has to produce one, and gives you a defensible expectation to judge your real Investopedia results against.

kits.evidence: A managed $100,000 Investopedia portfolio with at least one holding in each assigned vertical, plus the Excel model behind it: real price data, computed returns and volatility per holding, a Monte Carlo forecast with a percentile band, and a written defence of your allocation that was recorded BEFORE the outcome was known.
kits.stretch: Add correlation between two holdings and show how it changes the spread of outcomes — then say whether your actual portfolio was diversified or only looked diversified.

challenge.title: The Investopedia $100,000 Challenge
challenge.platform: Investopedia Stock Simulator (free account; the class joins one game)
rules: One holding minimum in each assigned vertical — you may not put it all in tech.
Every trade needs a recorded thesis BEFORE it is placed: why this company, what you expect, and what would prove you wrong.
You are graded on the quality of the reasoning and the model behind it, not on whether you beat the market. A well-argued loss outscores a lucky win.
No day trading. Positions are held and reviewed weekly.

kits.title: The Lemonade Stand
kits.premise: Everything so far, assembled into a business: demand you cannot control, costs you can, and a price you have to choose.

decks.title: Anatomy of a Business Model
decks.concept: Assumptions in, rules in the middle, outputs out. Once you can name those three layers in someone else's model, you can build your own — and every cornerstone so far has been practice for this.

decks.title: Break-Even & Sensitivity
decks.concept: Break-even is the question every business asks first. Sensitivity analysis asks the better second question: which assumption, if wrong, hurts most?

practicum.title: Business Model Practice
drills: Separate fixed from variable cost for a stand and compute contribution margin.
Solve break-even volume with a formula, then verify it by building the table.
Simulate demand as a function of price and weather.
Run a one-way sensitivity table on price; identify the profit-maximising price.
Run a two-way table (price × cup cost) and describe the shape of the surface.

tool.title: Virtual Lemonade Stand
tool.job: Business setup, inventory, daily operating log, forecast, and dashboard — a complete working engine. Students operate it, then reverse-engineer its rules into their own Excel model.

kits.evidence: A full business model: assumption block, simulated demand, cost structure, break-even, and a sensitivity analysis that identifies the assumption you would most want to be right about.
kits.stretch: Rebuild your model as a web app in the style of the Virtual Lemonade Stand — the same engine, your interface.

kits.title: The Pop-Up Forecast
kits.premise: Real data, real district, real pitch. Ten weeks to turn a question about the Design District into a forecast someone would fund.

decks.title: Real Data Is Dirty
decks.concept: Every dataset you have used until now was built for you. This one was not: missing values, inconsistent categories, and outliers that are sometimes errors and sometimes the whole story.

decks.title: Regression & Seasonality
decks.concept: Fit a line to explain, not to decorate. Then find the pattern that repeats — seasonality is why last July predicts next July better than last month does.

decks.title: Optimisation & the Pitch
decks.concept: Solver finds the best answer inside your constraints. The pitch explains why anyone should believe it — the model is only half the deliverable.

practicum.title: Cleaning, Regression & Solver Practice
drills: Clean a deliberately messy extract: blanks, duplicate categories, a mis-typed date column.
Fit a regression and interpret slope in the units of the problem, not in statistics vocabulary.
Separate trend from seasonality on a monthly series.
Set up Solver with an objective and two real constraints, and read the result critically.

tool.title: Design District Pop-Up Forecast
tool.job: Brand setup, break-even, scenario toggles, and three chart views. Sets the standard for what the capstone deliverable can look like.

kits.evidence: A forecast built on real Design District data: documented cleaning decisions, a regression with seasonality, an optimised scenario via Solver, and a pitch that states the recommendation, the assumptions, and the risk.
kits.stretch: Build a live web dashboard for your forecast in the style of the Pop-Up Forecast tool.
kits.blocked: The dataset is still a documented placeholder — `resources/csm-capstone-design-district.csv` has a header row only. Real foot-traffic or sales data is needed before Mar 30.
